extracted.intended_audience: people who want to follow, verify, or contribute Metamath proofs (mathematicians and interested non-specialists)
extracted.subtask_description: Understand and mechanically verify Metamath proofs in the set.mm database by applying substitution rules, respecting syntax and distinct-variable conditions, and using the Metamath tools to inspect hidden steps where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution is the fundamental proof rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The only rule you need to know in order to follow the symbol manipulations in a Metamath proof is substitution. Substitution consists of replacing the symbols for variables with expressions representing special cases of those variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitution is just writing down a specific example of a more general formula. All proof steps are derived by substitution (and checking equality/structure); focus on substitutions rather than meanings of symbols. The Metamath verifier ensures these substitutions are legal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitutions must be simultaneous
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitutions are simultaneous: each occurrence of a given variable in a referenced theorem must be replaced with the same expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if a referenced theorem's assertion has two occurrences of F, both must be replaced with the same expression. This prevents inconsistent local substitutions across occurrences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitute only into variables of the referenced theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitutions are made into the variables of the referenced theorem only, never into the variables of any proof step referenced in the Hyp column (of the theorem being proved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When figuring substitutions, pretend that all variables in the theorem being proved are constants; treat proof-step symbols as not directly substitutable. This clarifies which symbols are targets for substitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constants must match exactly; variables are distinguished by color/notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Constants (connectives and constant symbols like '(', ')', '+', '1', '2', '=') must match exactly and cannot be substituted; variables are colored and represent placeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colors: constants black, purple/class variables, blue/wff variables, red/setvar variables (colors optional in monochrome). When matching a referenced theorem, focus on whether a symbol is a variable or a constant and require exact match for constants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable kinds and their substitution eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three main variable kinds with distinct substitution rules: setvar variables (lowercase italic red) can be substituted only with another setvar variable (a single symbol); wff variables (italic Greek blue) can be substituted only with expressions qualifying as wffs; class variables (uppercase italic purple) can be substituted with class expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Setvar restriction prevents nonsense substitutions like replacing bound-variable positions with complex expressions. Class variables generalize setvar/wff and allow substituting objects like numbers or operation symbols. See the Theory of Classes for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal syntax requirement for substitutions
rubrics_metrics.description: You may substitute only expressions that qualify as the required syntactic type (class, wff, setvar). For example, '(1 + 1)' is a legal class but '(1 +' is not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One must 'prove' (or show the construction) that any expression to be substituted qualifies as the legal expression for that variable type. The web page suppresses many construction steps, but they can be displayed via the Metamath program (e.g., 'show proof ... /all') or inferred from 'Syntax hints'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct variable conditions restrict allowable substitutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain axioms (e.g., ax-5) and theorems impose distinct-variable conditions that prohibit some substitutions that would otherwise be syntactically legal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These distinct-variable restrictions are inherited by theorems according to the substitutions used in their proofs. They do not affect how you figure out substitutions for matching, but you must respect them for overall correctness; see Appendix 3 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof structure: sequence of substitution instances with hypotheses matching previous steps
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is a sequence of substitution instances of axioms and inference rules, where hypotheses of inference rules match previous steps in the sequence. The last step is the theorem (assertion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs may refer to earlier theorems for brevity but can in principle be expanded to references only to initial axioms and rules. Derived inference rules/deductions are allowed (they behave like inference rules with local hypotheses).

rubrics_metrics.name: When referenced theorem has no hypotheses, omit Hyp and proceed
rubrics_metrics.description: If the referenced theorem (or axiom or definition) has no hypotheses, the Hyp column is omitted and its assertion can be used immediately as a proof step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the normal shortening for axioms and hypothesis-free theorems; multiple hypotheses are repeated as needed when present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rename variables in referenced theorems to avoid confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: If the variables of a referenced theorem happen to have the same names as those in the theorem being proved, temporarily rename the variables in the referenced theorem before substituting expressions to avoid confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: rewrite ax-1 with χ, ψ instead of φ, ψ to make subsequent substitutions clearer. Renaming clarifies which occurrences are being substituted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of definitions and their treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions (e.g., df-bi, df-an, df-ex) are introduced to simplify presentation and may be treated as additional axioms for practical work; their syntax breakdowns are shown on their pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although definitions can be justified metatheoretically, for working with Metamath you may treat them as axioms. The web pages show detailed syntax for axioms and definitions where there is space; hidden construction steps for substitutions are often suppressed but retrievable via the Metamath program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metamath verifier ensures correctness; you can inspect hidden construction steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs in the database have been computer-verified by the Metamath verifier. Hidden construction steps (e.g., demonstrating that '(1 + 1)' is a legal class) are present in the database but suppressed on the web pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To see hidden steps use the Metamath program commands (e.g., 'save proof 2p2e4 /normal' then 'show proof 2p2e4 /all' or 'show proof <theorem> /detailed_step <n>'). Trust the verifier for correctness but inspect steps if you need full syntactic justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on syntactic manipulation, not semantic meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: When following Metamath proofs, you should focus only on whether symbols are variables or constants and on the mechanical substitutions, not on what the symbols 'mean'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'formalism' viewpoint treats mathematics as symbol manipulation; it makes it possible for non-experts to verify proofs mechanically. Studying a proof with unfamiliar symbols can help observe substitutions without preconceived meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class theory (class builders) extends the language to practical mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory of classes introduces class builders of the form {x | φ} and class variables (uppercase) to represent objects such as numbers or operations, enabling substitutions that the primitive setvar/wff language forbids directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Class variables let you represent numbers, operations, etc., as classes; every class is a collection of sets (possibly not itself a set). This definitional mechanism is used to make mathematics practical in Metamath while remaining reducible to primitives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setvar variables are restricted to single-symbol substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: A setvar variable can be substituted only with another setvar variable (an expression of length one), since there are no rules that construct more complex setvar expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restriction preserves the role of setvar variables as bound/dummy variables (e.g., first argument of ∀) and prevents nonsensical substitutions like replacing 'x' with '2' in contexts where that would break binding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wff construction rules define allowable wff forms
rubrics_metrics.description: A wff (well-formed formula) is constructed by base forms (wff variable or x = y or x ∈ y) and then closed under →, ¬, and ∀ x; these construction rules determine which expressions can be substituted for wff variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarity with the wff construction rules helps you tell whether a candidate expression qualifies as a wff; pages describing individual axioms show syntax breakdowns to illustrate these rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical reading & tooling conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof pages use a Unicode math font by default, with a GIF alternate for browsers with poor Unicode rendering; ASCII token equivalents are provided for text-only browsers. The main font is left unspecified so readers may select comfortable fonts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Unicode renders poorly, switch to GIF version or use ASCII tokens. Text browsers (w3m, Lynx) can be used; CLI Metamath is recommended for accessibility and detailed inspection (e.g., for blind users).
